problems.title: Global loads per FMA
problems.solution: 0.125 and 0.0625: each value loaded is used T times.

problems.title: Shared memory per block
problems.statement: Tiles of A and B, T × T floats each.

problems.title: The tiled ceiling
problems.statement: Inner loop: two shared loads (one a broadcast) and one FMA per step.
problems.solution: 33% and 512 GFLOP/s. Tiling removed the global loads but kept an instruction per operand.

problems.title: Filling the machine
problems.statement: A 256 × 256 GEMM, one thread per output, T × T thread blocks. The GW-1 holds 2,048 threads and 16 blocks per SM, 16 SMs.
hints: T = 32 is 1,024 threads: 2 blocks per SM.
problems.solution: (a) 256 blocks. (b) 64. (c) 2 per SM × 16 = 32 per wave: 2 waves. Small problems can't use big tiles without losing parallelism.

problems.title: Tiled DRAM traffic
problems.statement: n = 4096, T = 32, and suppose L2 catches nothing between blocks.

parts.prompt: Bytes read for A and B?
Time for that traffic at 512 GB/s, in ms?

hints: Each element of A and B is read once per block-row or block-column: n/T times.
problems.solution: (a) $2 \times 4n^2 \times n/T = 17.2$ GB. (b) ≈ T/4 = 7.97. (c) 33.7 ms, against 89.5 ms of compute at peak: compute (and the 33% instruction ceiling) now dominates.

problems.title: Barriers
problems.solution: 32 steps, 64 barriers. Each barrier stalls the block until its slowest warp arrives; Chapter 4.4's double buffering removes one per step.

problems.title: The cost of an unknown trip count
problems.statement: The tiled inner loop written with k < T (a variable) instead of k < 16 (a literal) costs one extra branch instruction per iteration.

parts.prompt: FMA fraction with the literal bound, in %?
Slowdown if the kernel is issue-bound?

problems.solution: 3 versus 4 instructions per FMA: 33% versus 25%, a 1.33× slowdown from a loop the compiler couldn't unroll. Making tile sizes compile-time constants (templates in C++) matters.

problems.title: Block rasterisation
problems.statement: An n = 4096 GEMM with 256 × 256 block tiles: a 16 × 16 grid of tiles. 16 blocks run at once. Each block needs one row-panel of A and one column-panel of B.

parts.prompt: Distinct panels needed by a wave launched in row-major order (one row of tiles)?
By a wave arranged as a 4 × 4 group of tiles?

hints: Row-major: one A panel, 16 B panels.
problems.solution: (a) 17. (b) 8. Grouped launch order roughly halves the distinct data a wave pulls through L2, so more of it hits. CUTLASS calls this swizzling the block index; Triton exposes it as GROUP_SIZE_M.

problems.title: Occupancy of a tiled kernel
problems.statement: T = 32 (1,024-thread blocks), 32 registers per thread, 8 KB of shared memory, on the GW-1.
problems.solution: 2 blocks (the 64-warp limit), 100% occupancy, with shared memory to spare. Occupancy isn't this kernel's problem; instruction count is.

problems.title: What tiling doesn't fix

parts.prompt: …what still limits the kernel to about a third of peak?
options: Each FMA still needs operand loads as separate instructions

problems.solution: Operands from shared memory still cost an instruction each. Only register reuse (4.3) changes the ratio.
